title: Dining capacity decides your week.
subtitle: Not the number of restaurants — the number of seats behind the door.

text: Cabins are easy to add. Restaurant seats are not.
sub: That gap is why a celebrated ship can feel crowded at eight in the evening and completely empty at three in the afternoon.

points.label: Venue count
points.value: Ten restaurants sounds generous until you notice how few seats most of them hold.

points.label: Reservation windows
points.value: The earlier the booking opens, the more it is rationing something scarce.

points.label: Open or fixed dining
points.value: Open seating is a promise about capacity. Fixed seating is an admission about it.

points.label: The surcharge
points.value: A cover charge is often crowd control wearing a wine list.

left.label: Rationed
items: Book on day one or not at all
Cover charges on the good ones

right.label: Open
items: Room service that is real food

title: Three questions for the dining room

items.head: Seats, not venues
items.body: Ask for the seat count set against the guest count. Very few travellers ever do, and it is the number that matters.

items.head: When do bookings open
items.body: If specialty dining opens months out and vanishes in a morning, you have your answer already.

items.head: What room service is
items.body: On the best small ships it is the same kitchen and the same menu. Elsewhere it is sandwiches.

text: The best-designed ships remove the reservation entirely.
sub: No booking window, no cover charge, no scramble on embarkation afternoon. You simply go to dinner. It sounds trivial until you have had the other version.

title: Save this before you book a celebrated ship
body: Or send me the ship and I'll tell you whether dinner aboard is a pleasure or a project.
